Illustrated approach / source traceability

DSM-II: the short guide

Follow the power from the engine, through distributed plume sources, to each receiver. The excerpts below are actual figures from the cited references; the notes explain the choices made in this implementation.

Default approach · DSM-II distributed slices · Eldred core relation · 0.5% acoustic efficiency · energy normalization · free plume until a deflector is specified.

Run a prediction to show its source-power and geometry summary here.

1. Power & core2. Source power3. Slice spectra4. Deflector5. Propagation6. Sum & check
01 / establish the scale

Start with acoustic power and a core length

  • Power: use per-engine thrust F, exhaust velocity U, engine count N and efficiency η. The approximation is W = (η/100) N F U / 2; η is entered in percent.
  • Read the figure: increasing exit Mach number lengthens the aerodynamic core reference. Its length sets where DSM-II places acoustic power along the plume.
  • In this tool: Lc,free = C Deff(1 + 0.38 M)². C = 3.45 is the Eldred default; C = 1.75 is the Varnier / Haynes–Kenny sensitivity option.
  • Keep the inputs consistent: merged clusters use Deff = D√N; independent, co-located engines use D. Neither resolves individual nozzle spacing.
Example: with D = 1 m and M = 3.4, the free core is 18.12 m with Eldred or 9.19 m with Varnier. With F = 1 MN, U = 2800 m/s, N = 1 and η = 0.5%, acoustic power is 7.00 MW.

SP-8072 Eq. 1 corresponds to 1% efficiency; 0.5% is the nominal starting choice used here. A shorter core is a modeling choice, not a universal accuracy improvement.

02 / distribute acoustic power

Divide the plume into radiating slices

  • Read the axes: horizontal position is distance along the plume divided by core length. The vertical axis is a logarithmic power density per unit normalized length, not the power of a single slice.
  • In this tool: integrate the digitized historical curve from 0.1 to 5 core lengths. The receiver calculation uses the requested slices (240 by default); the field map uses 60.
  • Convert before summing: each slice receives power proportional to 10G(q)/10 Δq, with q = s/Lc. Power normalization makes all slice weights sum to one.
  • Location matters: moving this distribution changes source-to-receiver distances, angles and the frequencies assigned to the sources.

Historical limitation: Gee (2021) traced a plotting error into this Figure 12 distribution. This tool retains the curve for a transparent heritage DSM-II calculation. Normalization repairs its energy balance, not its physical provenance. Read the finding.

03 / assign frequencies to each slice

Each source radiates a full spectrum

  • Read the figure: the horizontal variable is the modified axial Strouhal number. The symbols show the experimental scatter around the empirical spectral shape.
  • Map to frequency: this tool uses Stx = f s / (M c₀), where s is distance along the plume and c₀ is ambient sound speed. The paper's x is that along-flow distance, not necessarily the map's horizontal coordinate after a bend.
  • Integrate band power: the curve is a spectral density. Integrate across the actual third-octave edges, then multiply by the slice power; do not treat a point on the curve as a band level.
  • Normalize the full spectrum: power outside the selected bands stays outside. The displayed bands are never rescaled to contain all acoustic power.
Example: at s = 20 m, M = 3.4 and c₀ = 343 m/s, Stx = 1 corresponds to f ≈ 58.3 Hz. Moving sources upstream raises the frequency associated with the same dimensionless spectral feature.
04 / account for the assumed flow path

A bend and core termination do different things

  1. Place the deflector: enter nozzle-to-deflector distance d. A value of zero means no deflector.
  2. Turn the centerline: β rotates the outgoing plume from +x toward +y. β = 90° sends it along +y. This is the plume turn angle, not a plate inclination.
  3. Choose core behavior: without termination, Lc remains the free core length. With termination, Lc = min(Lc,free, d); the source distribution and spectral scale then move accordingly.
  4. Inspect the geometry graphic: it reports d, β, the free/effective core lengths and the modeled source extent along the path.

The published illustration is drawn vertically. Our coordinates rotate the initial exhaust to +x. The tool uses a sharp, piecewise-straight centerline; it does not calculate a curved deflector surface, impingement noise, shielding or water suppression.

05 / propagate to a receiver

Distance and viewing angle both matter

  • For each slice: calculate distance r to the receiver and angle θ from the slice's local downstream flow tangent. After a bend, that tangent follows the outgoing plume.
  • Read the curves: directivity varies with both θ and ordinary Strouhal number f Deff/U. The loudest direction is not the same at every frequency.
  • Apply spreading: subtract 10 log₁₀(4πr²) from source band power level, then add directivity, the selected propagation-loss term and one reflection correction.
  • Respect the domain: the heritage interpolation holds outside Sr = 0.004–0.4 and θ = 20–180°, with a warning. SATURN directivity supports only θ = 0–90°.

Using far-field directivity for individual near-field slices is an empirical approximation acknowledged by the original report. The separate directivity chart lets you inspect the implemented curve for each band.

06 / sum energy and check the evidence

Separate prediction, numerical checks and measured evidence

  1. Within each band: add the uncorrelated slice contributions in linear mean-square pressure, then convert to dB.
  2. Across bands: repeat that energy sum for OASPL. Apply band-center A-weighting for dBA. The user allowance is added separately to the design level.
  3. Read the published comparison: the Saturn V data show why core termination can matter in a specific launch geometry. They do not establish a universal correction for every engine.
  4. Check this implementation: numerical checks verify its equations and energy accounting. An exact measured replication still needs complete engine, geometry and measurement inputs.

Evidence boundary: the adjacent plot is a result from the paper, not output from this tool or a passed validation case. Its measurements are at the 85 m vehicle station. Our independent checks are documented in .

Which research options should I compare?

  • Core relation: compare Eldred and Varnier rather than assuming the shorter core is always better. James et al. (2016) found full-scale overall-level support for the original relationship in their solid-motor comparisons.
  • Core termination: compare preserved and terminated cores when a deflector is present; distinguish this from simply changing the flow direction.
  • Modern stationary model: Mathews' SATURN components use a measured-spectrum fit, s/D = 9.85 Sr⁻⁰·²¹ and a released Atlas V directivity dataset. This is a separate source model, not a correction to Figure 12.
  • Propagation: the optional SATURN empirical loss uses the released code's parameters. It is not a weather-specific, nonlinear or terrain propagation model.
Detailed equations, implementation choices and remaining limitations
W = (η/100) N F U / 2   [W]
Lw = 10 log₁₀(W / 10⁻¹²)   [dB re 1 pW]
Lp,b = 10 log₁₀ Σₛ { (Ws,b / 10⁻¹²) / (4πrₛ²) × 10^[(DIₛ,b + Aₛ,b + C)/10] }
Lp,overall = 10 log₁₀ Σᵦ 10^(Lp,b / 10)

The standard SP-8072 pressure/intensity reference convention is retained (ρc ≈ 400 Pa·s/m); 10 log₁₀(4π) = 10.992 dB replaces the report's rounded 11 dB. No atmospheric-impedance correction is applied.

Heritage models

  • DSM-I: Sr = f D/U. Integrate Figure 5's density across each band; place the band at the Figure 14 solid-line apparent source position. That historical preferred curve includes open-scoop data and is not a pure universal free-jet fit.
  • DSM-II: Lc = 3.45 D (1 + 0.38 M)². Use Figure 12 over 0.1–5 Lc, with midpoint slices, and Figure 13 using modified Sr = f x / (M c₀).
  • Normalization: independently normalize the full spectral distributions and the truncated axial distribution when selected. The displayed band range is never normalized to contain all power. Turn normalization off for a closer raw-curve comparison.
  • Digitization: Figures 5, 10, 12, 13 and 14 are approximate readings of scanned curves, not numerical measurements. Allow roughly 1 dB of curve-reading precision and about 10% in location, in addition to model uncertainty.

Research options

  • Varnier / Haynes–Kenny: alternative core coefficient 1.75. For DSM-II only, an idealized bend and optional core termination are available. Engine-specific RSRM directivity is not included.
  • SATURN stationary adaptation: uses Mathews' piecewise spectral density, s/D = 9.85 Sr⁻⁰·²¹, and the released Atlas V directivity table. It does not include launch trajectories, retarded time or plume-emergence masking.
  • SATURN propagation: uses the pinned code's 16 Hz and 8000 Hz loss parameters. The dissertation's printed equations differ; the audit records those discrepancies.
  • Modern directivity domain: the released table covers only 0–90° from downstream. Out-of-angle predictions are rejected; the map leaves those cells blank. Sr outside the table is held at its boundary and flagged.

What the literature changes—and what it does not establish

  1. 2001 / 2009: shorter cores and deflector effects. Varnier and Haynes–Kenny motivate core shortening and core termination for specific configurations. These are exposed as separate sensitivity controls.
  2. 2016: full-scale evidence challenges a universal shorter core. James and colleagues found overall-level support for the original core relationship across four full-scale solid motors, while spectra remained imperfect. A shorter core is therefore not the default “accuracy upgrade.”
  3. 2021: an inherited source-distribution error. Gee traced SP-8072 Figure 12 to a plotting error in earlier jet experiments. The corrected laboratory-jet distribution cannot by itself establish a universal hot-rocket distribution. DSM-II is retained and clearly labeled as historical; no invented correction curve is substituted.
  4. 2022–2024: source physics and installation matter. Reviews and measurements emphasize distributed/coherent sources, nonlinear propagation, impingement, ground effects, and water suppression. These cannot reliably be represented by a universal dB correction.
  5. 2025: modern measured spectrum and directivity. Mathews' SATURN framework provides published formulas and a reusable dataset. Its reported launch-validation errors depend on the complete model and datasets; they do not transfer to this stationary implementation.

Limits that affect interpretation

  • Stationary chemical-rocket broadband mixing-noise estimate. No ignition overpressure, discrete tones, combustion instability, shock-associated-noise separation, structural response or transient peak pressure.
  • No nonlinear propagation, refraction, terrain, shielding, water-injection physics, weather profile, ground impedance or coherent interference model.
  • Merged clusters use D√N. Independent clusters sum uncorrelated, co-located engine powers using D. Neither resolves actual nozzle spacing or azimuthal cluster asymmetry.
  • A-weighted levels are band-center estimates. “Overall” always means the selected band edges, not all frequencies. The map uses the same band scope.
  • Reflection choices are idealized +0, +3.01 or +6.02 dB. They are mutually exclusive; applying both ground doubling and pressure doubling would double-count effects.
  • Core-length controls affect DSM-II only. Bent centerlines do not constitute validated deflector or launch-pad simulation.

Primary references

  1. Eldred (1971), NASA SP-8072: Acoustic Loads Generated by the Propulsion System. Section 4.2, Eqs. 1–10; Figures 5, 10–14.
  2. Haynes & Kenny (2009), Modifications to SP-8072 Distributed Source Method II. Core, termination and RSRM directivity.
  3. James et al. (2016), Comparative Analysis of SP-8072's Core Length with Full-Scale Rocket Data.
  4. Gee (2021), A tale of two curves and their influence on rocket and supersonic jet noise research.
  5. Lubert, Gee & Tsutsumi (2022), Supersonic jet noise from launch vehicles: 50 years since NASA SP-8072.
  6. Review of launcher lift-off noise prediction and mitigation (2024).
  7. Mathews (2025), Acoustic Characterization and Modeling…, Chapter 6 and Appendix B; pinned SATURN source and dataset.
  8. Perez & Allgood (2011), Prediction of Acoustic Loads Generated by Propulsion Systems. Published Stennis verification/validation cases, Tables 2–4.
  9. Smith III (2013), An Empirical and Computational Investigation into the Acoustical Environment at the Launch of a Space Vehicle. Section 3.4, Tables 8-10, Figure 53. Laboratory-jet comparison; see Verification & audit for directivity differences and the Appendix D quadrant error.
  10. Fukuda et al. (2011), An Acoustic Impedance Model for Evaluating the Ground Effect of Static-Firing Tests on a Rocket Motor. Figures 17–18: original and ground-corrected measured spectra; input conditions from Tsutsumi et al. (2009). See the NAL-735 measured-data assessment in Verification & audit.

Technical assurance

Verification is layered

Equation checks, numerical cross-checks and measured validation answer different questions. The distinction is preserved here.

Measured spectra · independent test campaign

JAXA NAL-735 · Noshiro static firing

A 260 kN solid rocket tested in December 2007. Fukuda et al. (2011), Figures 17–18, publish measured spectra at M1 (80° arc) and M8 (near field), together with two model-based ground corrections. These are experimental observations, separate from the Smith prediction replay.

Fixed case, independent of calculator edits. No efficiency, level offset, core length or directivity is fitted to the measured curves. Loading replaces calculator inputs and the pinned comparison with M1’s σ = 5,000 corrected measurement.

Measured-data assessment with declared assumptions. Free-field predictions are assessed against both author ground-corrected curves. Raw measurements are shown separately because they include reflections. The ground correction itself uses an assumed source distribution; it is not an independent free-field measurement. This case assesses accuracy without establishing a general validation pass.

ReceiverRMS · correction ARMS · correction BLargest residual · A / BBias · A / B

All metrics in dB, nominal 125–2,000 Hz, 13 bands per receiver. A: published σ = 5,000; B: σ = 200,000 kPa·s/m². These are two ground-model scenarios, not a statistical confidence interval. Positive residual means the calculator is higher.

Why this case is useful—and what remains uncertain
  1. Published motor inputs: thrust 260 kN, exit diameter 0.614 m, exit Mach 2.92. Tsutsumi et al. (2009), Table 1, also report overexpansion Pe/Pa = 0.418 and fully expanded diameter/Mach of 0.446 m / 2.47. The baseline consistently uses exit diameter/Mach with the Eldred core.
  2. Derived and assumed inputs: exit velocity ≈2,456 m/s follows from the published frequency/Strouhal mapping (4,000 Hz at Sr = 1). Ambient sound speed 343 m/s is assumed. Acoustic efficiency 0.84% is the companion paper’s Sutherland-based estimate, not a fit here. We use the calculator’s ½FU power convention; the paper uses fully expanded kinetic power, so this is an assessment of our documented model, not exact replication of their prediction.
  3. Geometry: M1 lies on a 39 m radius at 80° from the downstream axis. M8 is 10 m downstream and 13 m laterally offset. Nozzle/microphone heights are 1.8 m and 1.45 / 0.12 m. Height differences are folded into the radial distance for this straight axisymmetric plume. The 2011 prose calls 39 m a diameter; the 2009 paper and diagrams identify it as the radius.
  4. Fixed assessment choices: DSM-II, Eldred core, normalized historical source curves, legacy directivity, 240 slices, zero reflection, no extra propagation loss and no design margin. The published ground corrections are retained as data; no second reflection adjustment is applied.
  5. Scope: two receivers and 13 assessed bands each provide a real test of spectral shape and spatial prediction. Ground correction, overexpanded flow, acoustic-efficiency uncertainty and empirical near-field limitations prevent a clean universal accuracy claim. Above 2 kHz, retained readings are diagnostic only.
Original measured figures and sources
Published spectrum comparison · reconstruction

Smith 2013 · published laboratory-jet comparison

Section 3.4 supplies the laboratory air-jet inputs; Figure 53 supplies the predicted spectrum at the 45° receiver. The audit traces the discrepancy to model choices and an angle error in the publication’s appended code. This is a diagnostic reconstruction, not a full-scale rocket validation.

This panel always runs the fixed reference case, independently of calculator edits. Loading the case replaces the calculator inputs and its pinned comparison.

Discrepancy traced — not a verification pass. Replaying Smith’s formulas and the appended code’s angle error reproduces the plotted curve within its estimated reading precision. The error is confined to this diagnostic replay; the calculator retains physical angles. No efficiency or vertical offset was fitted.

Workbench DSM-IISmith Fig. 53 · published predictionDiagnostic replay · includes source angle error

One-third-octave SPL, dB re 20 µPa. Published red SPL curve sampled at 21 workbench centers, 100–10,000 Hz. The paper’s blue spectrum-density curve and measured circles are excluded. Source uses base-2 centers; this curve interpolation onto base-10 centers is approximate. Estimated graph-reading precision: ±0.5 dB, not a model uncertainty.

Where the difference comes from

Each row adds one change to the preceding row. RMS values summarize all 21 band differences; they are not additive corrections. The final reconstruction retains our source grid, receiver coordinates and 14 W acoustic power.

Cumulative diagnostic changeRMS · dBMean · dB100 Hz change · dB
  1. Different directivity: Smith uses Wilby III; the calculator baseline uses Eldred’s Figure 10. These are different empirical models. Smith extends Wilby below its stated 90°–180° domain.
  2. Angle error in the appended code: Appendix D, printed p. 262, uses a one-argument arctangent that loses the quadrant. Its straight-jet calculation gives angles above 180° for this downstream receiver and incorrectly activates Wilby’s low-frequency correction intended for angles ≥170°. Our calculator uses the plume tangent and receiver vector, giving angles in 0°–180°.
  3. Smaller conventions: unnormalized analytical fits and center-density × base-2 bandwidth account for the remaining difference. They are reproduced only in this audit.

The close match strongly implicates the published angle calculation, but the original saved run is unavailable. This is a reconstruction of its behavior, not an exact execution of the dissertation software. Correcting that angle alone would move the low-frequency result away from the printed curve.

The physical-angle alternative uses Wilby III outside its original angular domain; it is a diagnostic sensitivity, not a recommended rocket model.

Inputs, assumptions and comparison limits
  1. Published inputs: thrust 794.3 N; velocity 406.6 m/s; diameter 0.073 m; Mach 1.15; one nozzle; acoustic power 14 W (Table 9). The equivalent efficiency is 0.008670%; this encodes the paper’s power assumption.
  2. Geometry: free jet; receiver (+3.5, 3.5) m in our coordinates, corresponding to the paper’s Z = −3.5 m. Its nozzle distance is 4.950 m; 3.5 m is the transverse offset. Sound speed 353.50 m/s is derived from 311 K using ideal air.
  3. Workbench choices: Eldred core, normalized historical curves, 240 slices over 0.1–5 core lengths, no reflection or extra propagation loss. The audit retains that source grid. Smith’s exact saved small-jet discretization is unavailable. Appendix D’s external Proudman data branch is consistent with the later CFD study (Section 5.3, printed p. 123); it is not needed to reconstruct the Chapter 3 curve with the empirical fits.
  4. What this checks: published-curve reconstruction and discrepancy attribution. The baseline’s 13.11 dB value is an RMS difference across bands, not a uniform offset or an OASPL error. No error was found in the calculator’s angle or power summation. The low-speed jet is outside standard chemical-rocket conditions, and Table 10’s broader-band OASPL is not an acceptance target.
Inspect the original figure and provenance

Published numerical benchmark

NASA Stennis' 2011 report, Table 3, gives acoustic power 10.58 MW and sound power level 190.25 dB re 1 pW. This is a directly reproducible check of the power-to-level conversion.

Independent numerical verification

  • A separate Python/SciPy reference integrates spectra by adaptive quadrature and interpolates the original released SATURN directivity data.
  • Fixed frequency/location cases check spectrum normalization, source positions, geometric spreading, angle conventions, directivity, empirical propagation and pressure summation.
  • Automated invariants check thrust/efficiency scaling, inverse-square spreading, reflection corrections, cluster conventions, frequency coverage, DSM-II slice convergence and input rejection.
  • Browser checks exercise offline startup, each model, all charts, case round trips, stale results, exports and narrow-screen layout.

Secondary technical audit

  1. Power and reference units: η is a percentage in the interface and a fraction in the equation. W uses total engine power; dB references are 1 pW and 20 µPa.
  2. Published equation discrepancies: Mathews Eq. 6.5 prints a negative de-normalization expression and Eq. 6.10 adds a positive spreading term. This implementation follows dimensional analysis and the released code: add source level, subtract spreading loss.
  3. Propagation version: the released code uses f₁ = 16 Hz, n₁ = √(r/12000), f₂ = 8000 Hz, n₂ = (r/3000)¹·⁵. The dissertation prints different parameters. No silent mixture of those formulations is used.
  4. Band energy: spectral densities are integrated over exact base-10 third-octave edges; they are not mistaken for band powers. All sources are summed in linear energy.
  5. Domain controls: unsupported modern directivity angles produce errors or masked map cells, rather than uncontrolled extrapolation. Source coincidences are rejected.
  6. Known heritage uncertainty: the Figure 12 error and manual digitization remain explicit limitations. Normalization fixes energy balance, not the underlying physical source distribution.

Experimental cases found

  • NASA Stennis 2011: a 400 klbf LOX/RP engine with published input ratios and measured/predicted spectra. The paper reports DSM-I near-field levels around 143.1 dB and DSM-II around 149.5 dB. Exact flow dimensions, deflector geometry, ad-hoc source placement and custom curves are incomplete, so those receiver levels are not presented as a passed replication.
  • Haynes–Kenny 2009: Saturn V measured spectra at vehicle stations 85 m and 45 m from the nozzle compare full and terminated cores. Useful physical evidence, but insufficient complete inputs for an exact independently reproducible case here.
  • Mathews 2025: Firefly Alpha and Starship launch comparisons provide modern experimental evidence. Raw flight trajectories and all measurement histories are not in the pinned repository. This stationary application does not claim that validation.

Release status: numerical/software verification supports correct execution of the documented model. End-to-end experimental validation for an actual engine and facility remains open. See the delivered technical audit for test results and reproducibility instructions.
